# Tolstoy

> Tolstoy (gotolstoy.com) is the AI-native commerce platform: an AI agent that creates
> ecommerce content, runs shoppable video experiences, manages ads, and powers guided
> shopping for Shopify and ecommerce brands.

## Products

- [Shop Bots](https://www.gotolstoy.com/bots): AI employees for your brand — a Creative Director, Ecommerce Manager and Ads Manager, plus retail Shop Bots, with Tolstoy Enterprise for custom requirements.
- [Media Studio](https://www.gotolstoy.com/product/ai-studio) (formerly AI Studio): AI content creation for ecommerce — product videos, model photos, UGC-style video ads, try-on, PDP and lifestyle images, generated from the synced catalog and brand context.
- [Ads Studio](https://www.gotolstoy.com/product/ads-studio): create ad creative from products, publish approved Meta campaigns, and use performance to shape the next test.
- [Shoppable video](https://www.gotolstoy.com/shoppable-video): shoppable video for Shopify product pages, collections and homepages (part of Storefront Studio).
- [Virtual try-on](https://www.gotolstoy.com/product/virtual-try-on-studio): on-model try-on for apparel and accessories (part of Storefront Studio).
- [AI UGC](https://www.gotolstoy.com/ai-ugc): AI-generated, creator-style UGC for ecommerce ads and product pages.
- [AI product photography](https://www.gotolstoy.com/ai-product-photography): reviewable on-model, lifestyle, PDP, and campaign image workflows from product and brand inputs in Media Studio.
- [AI Player](https://www.gotolstoy.com/product/ai-player): shoppable video widgets for storefronts (stories, carousels, spotlight, hero).
- [AI Sales Agent](https://www.gotolstoy.com/product/ai-shopper): guided shopping agent and virtual try-on for storefronts.

## Industries

- [Industries](https://www.gotolstoy.com/industries): Tolstoy workflows, examples, templates, and customer evidence by ecommerce vertical.
- [Fashion](https://www.gotolstoy.com/industries/fashion): on-model creative, product video, visual discovery, and shoppable fashion experiences.
- [Beauty](https://www.gotolstoy.com/industries/beauty): product scenes, swatches, demos, UGC-style video, and shoppable PDP stories.
- [Jewelry](https://www.gotolstoy.com/industries/jewelry): macro concepts, worn-product creative, styling video, and shoppable product stories.
- [Food & beverage](https://www.gotolstoy.com/industries/food-beverage): product scenes, recipes, routines, creator ads, and interactive education.
- [Home](https://www.gotolstoy.com/industries/home): room scenes, product video, demonstrations, and shoppable home-content experiences.

## Resources

- [AI Commerce 2030](https://www.gotolstoy.com/research/ai-commerce-2030): an interactive US online retail scenario model, with five local assumptions, source notes, and practical Shop Bots, AI Photoshoots and Ads Studio workflows for fashion and beauty. Scenarios are illustrative, not forecasts or Tolstoy performance claims.
- [E-commerce analytics: what to measure and benchmarks by vertical](https://www.gotolstoy.com/blog/ecommerce-analytics-what-to-measure-benchmarks-by-vertical): store-level median AOV by vertical from Tolstoy store data (orders 2026-08-18 to 2026-11-15) and median refund rate by vertical (orders 2026-08-18 to 2026-10-16, refunds counted to 2026-11-15), read 2026-11-16, with store counts, population and definitions, plus which store metrics to measure and what event and shopper counts can and cannot show.

- [Playbooks](https://www.gotolstoy.com/playbooks): step-by-step ecommerce AI workflows for product photos, video and UGC, paid ads, storefront widgets, email and reporting, each with an /playbooks/<slug> page listing inputs, steps, outputs, the prompt or routine schedule, and a link that opens it in Tolstoy.
- [Templates & gallery](https://www.gotolstoy.com/templates): 300+ ready-to-use AI templates for ecommerce — UGC-style video ads, product videos, try-on, PDP and lifestyle images — plus a Made with Tolstoy gallery of AI-generated product image, video, UGC, ad, PDP, and lifestyle examples — each with its own /gallery/<slug> page.
- Gallery collections: [AI UGC examples](https://www.gotolstoy.com/gallery/ai-ugc-examples), [AI video ad examples](https://www.gotolstoy.com/gallery/ai-video-ad-examples), [AI fashion editorial examples](https://www.gotolstoy.com/gallery/ai-fashion-editorial-examples), [AI product hero shot examples](https://www.gotolstoy.com/gallery/ai-product-hero-examples) and [AI lifestyle product photo examples](https://www.gotolstoy.com/gallery/ai-lifestyle-product-examples), each listing every example of that use case with what makes it work.
- [AI models](https://www.gotolstoy.com/ai-models): generative models available in Media Studio (video: Seedance 2.0, Kling 3.0; image: Nano Banana Pro, Seedream 5 Pro, Grok Imagine, ChatGPT Images; and more), each with an /ai-models/<slug> page covering its ecommerce use cases.
- [Alternatives & comparisons](https://www.gotolstoy.com/alternatives): side-by-side comparisons against video commerce, live shopping, and UGC platforms, each with an /alternatives/tolstoy-vs-<slug> page. Competitor claims are sourced from each vendor's own public documentation and dated; capabilities we could not verify are marked "Not documented" rather than asserted as missing.
- Shopify shoppable video app comparisons: [Tolstoy vs Reelfy](https://www.gotolstoy.com/alternatives/tolstoy-vs-reelfy), [Tolstoy vs Video Slider (Doran)](https://www.gotolstoy.com/alternatives/tolstoy-vs-video-slider) and [Tolstoy vs Vizup](https://www.gotolstoy.com/alternatives/tolstoy-vs-vizup), each checked against the vendor's Shopify App Store listing on November 1, 2026.
- Best alternatives guides: [Best Videowise alternatives for Shopify](https://www.gotolstoy.com/alternatives/videowise-alternatives), [Best Moast alternatives for Shopify](https://www.gotolstoy.com/alternatives/moast-alternatives), [Best Firework alternatives for Shopify brands](https://www.gotolstoy.com/alternatives/firework-alternatives) and [Best Bambuser alternatives for Shopify](https://www.gotolstoy.com/alternatives/bambuser-alternatives): ranked alternatives with when each fits and published pricing from each vendor's Shopify App Store listing or site, read November 1, 2026.
- [Compare](https://www.gotolstoy.com/compare): outcome-based comparisons of Tolstoy with ecommerce AI, video commerce, shopping agent, and creative automation tools; pairwise guides at /compare/tolstoy-vs-<slug>.
- [Shopify video apps compared](https://www.gotolstoy.com/compare/shopify-video-apps): compare Shopify video apps by job — PDP widget, media library, live selling, or create-to-commerce platform.
- [Shopify shoppable video compared](https://www.gotolstoy.com/compare/shopify-shoppable-video): compare shoppable video by PDP job — native media, tagged widget, gallery, or catalog-connected platform.
- [Shopify UGC apps compared](https://www.gotolstoy.com/compare/shopify-ugc-apps): compare UGC apps by job — post-purchase reviews, social galleries, or shoppable video.
- [Best AI sales agents for Shopify in 2026, compared](https://www.gotolstoy.com/compare/shopify-ai-sales-agents): Tolstoy AI Sales Agent, Rep AI, Tidio Lyro, Manifest AI, Zipchat, Octane AI, Chatty, Shopify Inbox and Sidekick, by job, channel, catalog data, published price and App Store rating, read Nov 1, 2026 (Rep AI pricing, channels and rating read Nov 17, 2026).
- AI video ad and UGC ad comparisons: [Tolstoy vs Creatify (2026): AI video ads for ecommerce](https://www.gotolstoy.com/compare/tolstoy-vs-creatify), [Tolstoy vs Arcads (2026): AI UGC ads compared](https://www.gotolstoy.com/compare/tolstoy-vs-arcads) and [Tolstoy vs Billo](https://www.gotolstoy.com/compare/tolstoy-vs-billo); Creatify and Arcads facts checked against each vendor's own site on November 1, 2026.
- AI content tool comparisons: [Tolstoy vs HeyGen](https://www.gotolstoy.com/compare/tolstoy-vs-heygen), [Tolstoy vs MakeUGC](https://www.gotolstoy.com/compare/tolstoy-vs-makeugc), [Tolstoy vs Photoroom](https://www.gotolstoy.com/compare/tolstoy-vs-photoroom), [Tolstoy vs Pebblely](https://www.gotolstoy.com/compare/tolstoy-vs-pebblely).
- [Blog](https://www.gotolstoy.com/blog): guides on AI commerce, shoppable video, UGC, and ecommerce content strategy.
- [Pricing](https://www.gotolstoy.com/pricing): Plans are priced per workspace. Extra team members cost $20 per seat per month, or $16 billed yearly. Plus: $20 a month billed monthly, or $16 a month billed yearly ($192 a year), with 3,000 Studio credits, 1,000 Onsite AI credits and 5,000 video viewers a month (extra viewers $10 / 1,000). Business has 3 usage levels: $100 a month billed monthly, or $80 a month billed yearly ($960 a year), with 15,000 Studio credits, 5,000 Onsite AI credits and 25,000 video viewers a month (extra viewers $7 / 1,000); $200 a month billed monthly, or $160 a month billed yearly ($1,920 a year), with 30,000 Studio credits, 10,000 Onsite AI credits and 50,000 video viewers a month (extra viewers $7 / 1,000); $500 a month billed monthly, or $400 a month billed yearly ($4,800 a year), with 75,000 Studio credits, 25,000 Onsite AI credits and 125,000 video viewers a month (extra viewers $5 / 1,000). Enterprise is custom: custom capacity, contracts and commercial requirements. Creating an account is free, and every account starts on the Free plan. E-commerce analytics (sending events and reading the report), the CLI and the MCP need no paid plan. Every paid plan includes Shop Bots, Media Studio, Ads Studio and Onsite AI (virtual try-on, shoppable video, Personal Shopper). Studio credits cover creation and workflows; Onsite AI credits cover shopper conversations and virtual try-on; video viewers are a separate allowance. Tolstoy Forward is included in Enterprise and available as a separately quoted add-on to Business; Plus is not eligible. Agency service fees and any partner arrangements are agreed separately.
- [Tolstoy Forward](https://www.gotolstoy.com/forward): A three-month engineering and operations guidance program scoped around your business. Included in Enterprise, or a separately quoted add-on to Business. A named Tolstoy lead helps your team build, launch and improve AI workflows, starting with a 90-minute executive kickoff, a day-to-day owner, an ROI baseline and a 90-day plan. Scope and commercial terms are agreed before kickoff. After the program, your team or agency can keep operating, or agree the next phase with Tolstoy. ROI is measured, not guaranteed. [Talk to us about Forward](https://www.gotolstoy.com/contact-sales?interest=tolstoy-forward).
- [Integrations](https://www.gotolstoy.com/integrations): current native connections, compatible commerce platforms, automation workflows, publishing channels, and MCP clients, with product and setup details.
- [Enterprise](https://www.gotolstoy.com/enterprise): custom plans, invoice billing, security-review support.
- [Contact sales](https://www.gotolstoy.com/contact-sales)

## Buyer guides

- [Best AI content creation tools for ecommerce](https://www.gotolstoy.com/blog/best-ai-content-creation-tools-ecommerce): images, video, ads and copy compared by job.
- [Best AI UGC ad generators for ecommerce](https://www.gotolstoy.com/blog/best-ai-ugc-ad-generators): UGC-style ad tools compared by output, pricing and fit.
- [Best AI video ad generators for ecommerce](https://www.gotolstoy.com/blog/best-ai-video-ad-generators-ecommerce): video ad tools compared by format, pricing and publishing.
- [Best AI product video generators for Shopify](https://www.gotolstoy.com/blog/best-ai-product-video-generators): tools that turn product photos into PDP videos and ads.
- [Product photography tools](https://www.gotolstoy.com/blog/product-photography-tools): tools for product photos and lifestyle images.
- [How to add shoppable video to Shopify](https://www.gotolstoy.com/blog/how-to-add-shoppable-video-to-shopify): step-by-step setup, from app install and catalog import to product tagging, theme publishing and measurement.
- [How to turn Instagram and TikTok videos into shoppable videos on Shopify](https://www.gotolstoy.com/blog/turn-instagram-tiktok-videos-into-shoppable-videos-shopify): import Reels and TikToks, get rights, tag products and publish them on product pages.
- [Free e-commerce analytics tools: PostHog, Plausible, GA4, Umami](https://www.gotolstoy.com/blog/free-ecommerce-analytics-tools-compared): what free covers in Tolstoy, PostHog, Plausible, Google Analytics, Umami, GoatCounter and Mixpanel (hosted free tier, trial or self-hosted), with custom events, funnels, revenue, data freshness and agent read access, from each vendor's own pages checked 2026-11-16.

## Trust

- [Security](https://www.gotolstoy.com/security): SOC 2 Type II audits, encryption, access control, responsible disclosure.
- [Trust & Safety](https://www.gotolstoy.com/trust-and-safety): consent-first avatars, prohibited uses, enforcement, brand control.

## Platform

- Customers sign in at https://platform.gotolstoy.com
- Shopify app: https://apps.shopify.com/tolstoy

## Developers

Connect Tolstoy to AI agents and assistants through MCP (Model Context Protocol). Full documentation: https://developers.gotolstoy.com

- [Developer hub](https://developers.gotolstoy.com/welcome): MCP and integration documentation for Tolstoy.
- [OpenAPI spec](https://www.gotolstoy.com/openapi.json): machine-readable description of the workspace API — operations, request and response schemas, and OAuth 2.0 authentication (scope `workspace`).
- MCP server (Model Context Protocol, Streamable HTTP transport): connect a client to `https://apilb.gotolstoy.com/mcp/v1/mcp` (workspace tools, OAuth sign-in). Client setup guides: https://www.gotolstoy.com/mcp
- CLI: [`@tolstoy-ai/cli`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@tolstoy-ai/cli) on npm. Run `npx @tolstoy-ai/cli` (binary `tolstoy`) to script your Tolstoy workspace; sign in with your Tolstoy API key.

- [Bot marketplace](https://www.gotolstoy.com/marketplace): Templates from the platform bot library, grouped by work and filterable by ecommerce team. Each bot links to shared team workflows with inputs, outputs, review steps and exact starter tasks. Use template opens the review screen; Start with this ShopBot starts the conversation.

# Team starter pack: Buying & Product Development
URL: https://www.gotolstoy.com/teams/buying-product-development
Summary: Bring a range to life from product flats and references. Explore artwork, compare colors and give marketing a clear picture of the looks to shoot.
Bot marketplace: https://www.gotolstoy.com/marketplace#team=buying
## Build a range presentation
Bring: 3–5 product flats, style names, color references and an approved model reference.
Make: A labeled range board and separate review images.
Review: Each style and color matches the source, with clear labels for the range review.
## Develop an artwork direction
Bring: Owned or approved inspiration, garment reference, technique and color palette.
Make: Three artwork directions and one selected garment visualization.
Review: The artwork follows the brief and the garment visualization reflects the selected direction.
## Prepare a marketing handover
Bring: The selected range, hero looks and campaign priorities.
Make: A key-look sheet matching styled looks to product flats and identifiers.
Review: Every outfit maps to the right product flat, style name and hero detail.

---

# Team starter pack: Creative & Brand
URL: https://www.gotolstoy.com/teams/creative-brand
Summary: Take a visual direction from the first reference to the last campaign placement. Keep the product, the brand and the story consistent.
Bot marketplace: https://www.gotolstoy.com/marketplace#team=creative
## Create a campaign direction
Bring: Campaign brief, actual product images, brand examples and intended placements.
Make: Two directions and a selected hero image.
Review: The direction fits the brand, and the product matches the reference.
Bot template: https://www.gotolstoy.com/marketplace/creative-director#workflow-campaign-direction
## Extend a product education series
Bring: One approved infographic and 3 product/color variants with verified facts.
Make: A consistent set of product-gallery images.
Review: Product facts, colors and materials remain accurate across all variants.
Bot template: https://www.gotolstoy.com/marketplace/creative-director#workflow-product-education-series

Bring: Approved hero asset, size list and placement references.
Make: A reviewed banner, email hero and social format.
Review: The product, model, crop and copy space work in each placement.

# Bot template: Creative Director
URL: https://www.gotolstoy.com/marketplace/creative-director
Category: Creative & content
Summary: Set the creative direction, create on-brand images, and check their quality.

First result: A visual direction for approval, followed by images checked against your brief and references.

Useful sources:
- Campaign brief
- Brand guidelines
- Product catalog
- Product, model, and style references

What this bot works on:
- Propose a visual direction
- Create and retouch images
- Check product accuracy and realism

Review requirements: Approve the visual direction before image creation. Review the images before any publication or scheduling.

Starter instructions: Act as my creative director. First check what you can already use: my brand guidelines and saved creative rules, my catalog, and images I’ve approved before. List the rules you’ll follow: formats and safe zones, headline style, backgrounds and props to avoid, and how to use references (as inspiration, never copies). Ask me to confirm them, then save them for every future batch. Propose one visual direction for my brief. Once I approve it, make a pilot of up to 5 images, check each against the rules and the real product, and tell me how many are ready to use and what you fixed. Tell me the credit cost before a larger batch. Don’t publish or schedule anything without my approval.

# Ad Guidelines

## Account details
Set up with the team when the bot starts. Until an item is set, ask before relying on it.
- Store, brands sold and markets: not set yet
- Fonts for the product name and other text: not set yet
- Safe-zone templates: not set yet (use the default content box under Safe zones)
- Where the original product photos are kept: not set yet
- Minimum stock a product needs before it is advertised, and where to read it: not set yet
- Product types that are never advertised: not set yet

## Workflow
When asked to generate ads:
1. Choose as many products as the person asks for, following Product selection.
2. For each product, find the best ad inspiration, following the References section of the Creative Guide.
3. Show the person the chosen inspiration for each product, with a few alternatives, on a review dashboard, and wait for their approval.
4. After approval, generate the ads from the approved references, then show the results on a review dashboard.

## Sizes
Each product gets two output sizes: 1080×1920 (Stories and Reels) and 1080×1350 (feed), at exactly those pixel sizes.

## Safe zones
The team's safe-zone templates mark where the app's interface covers the ad. Until the team gives its own, use this default content box:

- 1080×1920: red bands y0–190 and y1541–1919. Content box x45–1034, y255–1476.
- 1080×1350: red bands y0–134 and y1215–1349. Content box x40–1039, y200–1149.

The product, the logo and all text sit inside the content box. The red bands hold background only.

## Give the idea room
The image carries the ad's idea, and shoppers see it small, on a phone, scrolling past. Space the image doesn't use, like borders, panels or empty areas around it, makes the idea smaller and easier to scroll past. Use space that way only when it adds something to the idea.

## Readable logo and text
Each logo and line of text contrasts clearly with the pixels behind it in the finished image (check the image, not the prompt).

- **Logos on one line:** when the store's logo and the brand's logo appear together, their lettering shares one baseline and is about the same height. Line them up by the words, not by each logo's outer edges. Crests, icons and underlines can stick out above or below. A separator between them (such as × or |) is centred on the letters, measured by its actual shape. Logos placed in separate corners still share a baseline.
- **Product name:** set the product name so each letter stays distinct at the size shoppers see it, most of all in narrow, tightly spaced or heavy fonts.
- **Space around the subject:** the product is what the ad sells, so it needs room to be seen. Text and logos sit in space of their own, clearly apart from the product and any person. When they crowd the subject, the ad feels cramped and the product loses attention.

## What every ad shows
Every ad shows the product's name and the store's logo. When the product is another brand's, the ad also shows that brand's logo. The name comes from the product page and can be shortened, as long as it stays accurate. The two logos can sit together in a store × brand lockup or separately, wherever the design works best.

## One brand per ad
The ad shows one brand: the product's own, plus the store's when they differ.

## Real logos
A logo in the ad is the real file, scaled proportionally and placed onto the image. The image model garbles logos, so it doesn't draw them.

- Logo files: the store's logo from its brand settings, each brand's official logo, or an existing store × brand lockup from the media library.
- When a brand's logo isn't in the library yet, get its official logo once, save it to the media library as "LOGO <Brand> <Black|White>" and reuse it in every later run.

## Exact product
The product is the exact SKU and colourway. Compared with its original photos at a similar scale, its graphics, lettering, logos, stitching, construction, proportions and colour all match.

- The images given to the model for the product are its original photos, each wider than 1000px.
- Code only resizes, crops and places the logo and text; it doesn't redraw, sharpen or upscale the product.
- When the originals don't show a detail clearly enough to check (small print, numbers), the report says so.

## Product selection
1. A product has at least the minimum stock in Account details. If the usual source doesn't work, find another way to get the figure rather than stopping.
2. Product types in Account details are excluded. Discounted or offer-uncertain products are held unless they're picked on purpose.
3. Figures from different markets, and online and in-store figures, are kept separate. Missing data is reported as UNKNOWN, never as zero.
4. Look for new arrivals, confirmed upcoming launches, strong sellers, related SKUs from a winning range, restocks, gaps between store and online sales, and older full-price stock with little exposure.
5. Prefer fresh opportunities and promising variants of proven sellers. Repeat a previously advertised SKU when it still qualifies, there's a clear reason to promote it again now, and the proposed creative is meaningfully different. Prior advertising or lifetime spend alone does not disqualify it.
6. For each recommendation, explain in one line why this product makes sense now and what the proposed ad adds.

## Faces
A face can appear only if it can't be recognised: turned away, cropped, out of focus, in shadow, or too small to make out. The aim is that no ad ever shows a clear face by accident, because a generated face can look like a real person, and real people can complain that their face was used.

## Work structure
Give every product its own worker chat, named after the product.

Briefs to job and worker chats pass on facts and rules only: the product, why it was picked, its sources, the guidelines, what the person said, and problems found in earlier ads (product mismatches, safe-zone or rule breaks). Creative decisions belong to the chat doing the work. A brief gives no example searches, shot types, scenes, settings, headlines or looks, and doesn't describe earlier ideas to follow.

## Licensed artwork
Licensed artwork on a product is never altered, and no franchise characters, logos or text are added beyond what's printed on the product.


--- Creative Guide.md ---
# Creative Guide

## Goal
These are Meta ads for the store, made for its marketing team. A good ad is one a shopper would buy from: it looks like an ad the store or its competitors would run, it speaks the product's brand, and the product looks exactly like the real one.

## Creativity
Before planning, briefing or making any ad, load the creativity skill. Every job and worker brief says to do the same.

## Reading the brand
Work out each brand's look and feel yourself before making its ads: the store's own look, the brand's own site, and the ads of the store's competitors.

## References
For each ad, find one real photo or ad that suits the product, and make our own take on it: the two should clearly share an idea, but not look identical.
- **Finding it:** first learn the product: what it is, what makes it different, who it is for and the world its brand comes from. Then search broadly: the product's category with words like campaign, editorial or ad, without naming a scene, prop, setting or product feature. Look at what comes back with the product in mind; the idea comes from where a strong reference and this product meet. Narrow down only after that. The shortlist shows different ideas, not versions of one. Pinterest usually works best; the Meta Ad Library mostly returns catalogue ads.
- **Choosing it:** make sure the product can be clearly seen in it. Judge each option on two things together: how strong the image is, and how much it says about this product. A striking image that would suit any other product of its kind isn't the first pick, and neither is one that's about the product but weak as an image. Look through several options and pick the one that does both best.
- **Using it:** give it to the image model labelled as the image to follow closely. Keep its composition (where the product sits in the frame and how big it is), how the product is presented, the camera angle, the light and the kind of setting. Change only enough that it isn't identical: the exact location details, the props and the colour palette. The reference's products, logos and text never carry over, and our product comes from its original photos.
- **Faces:** a reference can show faces. In the final ad, any face follows the Faces rule in the Ad Guidelines.

## Product sources
Match the exact catalog product and colourway. Find its original photos where Account details says they are kept, import them, and open them to check product, colour, view and dimensions. When the originals can't be found, the product page's highest-resolution images are the fallback; label them PDP FALLBACK and say why.

## Review
Report what you made and any problem you see, in plain words. The reviewer guides the direction; when the person rejects a look without saying what they want, ask what they would expect to see instead.

# Playbook: Write ad hooks worth testing
URL: https://www.gotolstoy.com/playbooks/ad-hooks-worth-testing
Category: Paid ads | Works with: Shopify, Tolstoy AI Studio
Summary: Tolstoy writes eight ad hooks from your real product facts, pairs each with a shot you can make from your own media, and picks the two to test first.

What you need:
- One product from your connected catalog
- The audience the ad is for, in one line
- Product photos or videos in your Tolstoy library, so each shot uses media you already have (optional)

How it runs:
1. Name product and audience: You select the product and say who the ad speaks to. If the audience is missing, the agent asks for it before it writes.
2. Write eight hooks: The agent mixes a specific problem, a practical demonstration, a useful detail and a direct question, using only facts your catalog supports.
3. Pair each with a shot: Every hook gets one concrete opening shot that your products and media can produce.
4. Pick the top two: The agent recommends the two strongest hooks and says why, so you know which ones to test first.

What you get:
- Eight short opening hooks for one product and one audience
- One concrete visual shot for each hook
- The two hooks to test first, with a short reason for each

Check the result:
- The eight hooks differ from each other: a mix of problem, demonstration, detail and question, not eight versions of one line.
- You can make every shot today with the products and media you have.
- No hook claims a result, a review or a testimonial that your catalog does not support.

Limits:
- Text only: hooks, shot ideas and two picks. Making the video or the ad is a separate step, for example with the UGC video ads playbook.
- One product and one audience per run. For a second audience, run it again.

Prompt: Write eight short opening hooks for the product I select and the audience I describe. Use only facts supported by my catalog and the material I attach. If an essential input, such as the audience, is missing, ask only for that input before writing. Mix a specific problem, a practical demonstration, a useful detail and a direct question where they fit. Avoid empty superlatives, fake testimonials and invented performance claims. Pair each hook with one concrete visual shot that can be made from my available products and media. Recommend the strongest two and explain the choice briefly. Keep the real product shape, proportions, construction, print, color, logos and readable labels intact. Do not invent product features, claims or reviews.

FAQs:
Q: What makes an ad hook worth testing?
A: It names something specific: a problem the shopper has, a thing the product does on camera, a detail they would miss, or a question they would answer. A line such as "the best you will ever own" gives a test nothing to learn from.
Q: How many hooks should I test at once?
A: Start with the two the agent recommends. Keep the product, offer and body copy the same in both ads, so the hook is the only thing that changes. Keep the other six for the next round.
Q: Can I use the hooks on TikTok and Reels, not only Meta?
A: Yes. The hooks are opening lines and shots, not platform settings. Name the platform in your message if you want the wording to match how people talk there.

- Tolstoy widgets on your store, so each asset collects exposure and plays

How it runs:
1. Set the window: The routine compares the last 30 complete days with the 30 days before, and records the exact dates and metric definitions.
2. Pull asset performance: It reads exposure, plays, completion, interactions and attributed order credits for each asset, then matches each asset to its library record and product tags.
3. Group the creative: It groups assets only by recorded or visible attributes: a named model, a treatment such as on-model or lifestyle, and the format and aspect ratio.
4. Compare fairly: It ranks a group only with at least 3 assets and 100 exposures or plays, and keeps smaller groups as directional evidence.
5. Flag fatigue and plan tests: It marks an asset fatiguing only when its metric falls across two comparable weeks at meaningful exposure, then proposes three tests that each change one variable.

What you get:
- A table of winning signals by model or treatment, with sample size and confidence
- A fatigue and underperformance list with the measured signal for each item
- Three controlled next tests, plus notes on missing data and coverage

Check the result:
- Every row in the winning signals table shows its asset count, exposure or plays, and a confidence level.
- Each item on the fatigue list shows the measured signal and its sample, not only a low number.
- Each of the three tests changes one thing, such as the model or the background, and keeps the rest the same.

Limits:
- It reads and reports only. It does not publish, replace or remove content, and you choose which tests to run.
- It measures assets that shoppers see through Tolstoy widgets on your store. Results from your Meta ads are not in this report.
- Comparisons are descriptive, not causal. A winning model is a signal to test, not proof that it caused more sales.

Schedule: Every Monday at 11:00 in your time zone; you can change the time

FAQs:
Q: What is the difference between fatiguing and underperforming?
A: Fatiguing means the metric fell across at least two comparable weeks while exposure stayed meaningful. Low performance with no downward trend is marked underperforming instead.
Q: How does it know which model is in an image?
A: From the model name recorded in Tolstoy. It never guesses who a person is from how they look, so assets without a named model are grouped as "unknown model".
Q: What do I do with an asset marked fatiguing?
A: Run one of the suggested tests on it. Each test changes one variable, such as the model or the background, so the next report shows which change moved the metric.

# Playbook: Decide which Meta ads to kill, scale or refresh
URL: https://www.gotolstoy.com/playbooks/daily-meta-ad-decisions

Summary: Every morning, Tolstoy gives each active Meta ad one verdict (kill, scale, refresh or keep) with exact budget numbers, and drafts new concepts for tired ads.

How it runs:
1. Pull two weeks of data: The routine reads campaign, ad set and ad results for the last 7 days, compares them with the 7 days before, and reads ad set frequency.
2. Mark kills and scales: Kill means meaningful spend with no purchases, or ROAS under 1.0x, for 7 days; scale means ROAS above target, 5+ purchases and frequency under 3.
3. Flag tired ads: An ad is marked refresh when ad set frequency passes 3.5 or CTR falls for 3+ days while spend holds, and the agent drafts replacement concepts.
4. Write exact actions: Budget changes are exact dollar figures, at most 30% per step; ads in the learning phase are not killed, and ads under 3 purchases are not scaled.

What you get:
- A one-line account health summary: spend, ROAS and the change since yesterday
- Kill, scale, refresh and keep lists, with no more than two lines per ad
- 2–3 replacement creative concepts for each fatigued ad

Check the result:
- Check one kill line and one scale line against Meta Ads Manager for the same 7 days: spend, purchases and ROAS match.
- Every scale line gives a from-and-to daily budget no more than 30% above the current one.
- No ad under scale has fewer than 5 purchases, and no ad that meets the kill rule appears under refresh.

Limits:
- Report only. It does not pause ads, change budgets or launch the replacement concepts. You make the changes in Meta Ads Manager.
- It judges ads by their numbers, names and placements. It does not look at the creative itself.
- Meta ads only. Ads on other platforms are not in the list.

Schedule: Every day at 12:00 in your time zone; you can change the time

FAQs:
Q: How do I scale video ads for ecommerce without wasting budget?
A: Scale only the ads that have proved themselves, and in small steps. This routine marks an ad for scale when its ROAS is above your target, it has 5 or more purchases and its frequency is under 3, and it caps each budget increase at 30%. Ads with fewer than 3 purchases stay in keep, because the result is too early to trust.
Q: How does it decide an ad is fatigued?
A: An ad is marked for refresh when its ad set frequency is above 3.5, or when its click-through rate falls for three or more days while spend holds. Kill always wins over refresh, so an ad that loses money is not refreshed.
Q: Can I set my own ROAS target and spend threshold?
A: Yes. The routine prompt says "ROAS above target" and "meaningful spend" without fixed numbers. Write your numbers into the prompt when you set up the routine, or answer the setup chat when it asks for them.

# Playbook: Refresh a fatigued ad creative
URL: https://www.gotolstoy.com/playbooks/refresh-fatigued-ad-creative
Category: Paid ads | Works with: Shopify, Tolstoy AI Studio
Summary: Tolstoy turns a tired ad into two new versions that each change one element, such as the opening frame or background, to beat creative fatigue without a new shoot.

What you need:
- The ad creative you want to refresh, as an image or video file
- Performance notes, if you have them, such as frequency, click-through rate or the date results started to drop
- The product shown in the ad, from your connected catalog

How it runs:
1. Attach the tired ad: You upload the creative and any performance notes. Without data, the agent does not assume the original was a winner.
2. Change one element each: Each version changes one meaningful element, such as the opening frame, the framing or the background.
3. Keep what people know: The product, the offer and the brand look stay the same, so the ad looks new in the feed and still looks like your brand.
4. Match the original size: You get two assets at the original aspect ratio, each with a note that names the element it changes.

What you get:
- Two refreshed versions of the ad at the original aspect ratio
- A note for each version that names the one element it changes

Check the result:
- Put each version next to the original: the named change is visible at a glance, and nothing else moved.
- The product, logo, label text and offer are the same as in the original.
- Both versions have the aspect ratio of the original, so they fit the same placements.

Limits:
- A refresh keeps the concept. If the idea itself stopped working, test new angles instead.
- It works from the notes you type in. For a daily list of which ads are fatigued, use the daily Meta ad decisions routine.
- It does not replace the ad in Meta. You upload the new versions and run them next to the original.

Prompt: Refresh the ad creative I attach. Use any performance notes I give you, and do not assume the original performed well without data. If the creative is missing, ask only for it before generating. Make two refreshed versions that each change one meaningful element, such as the opening frame, framing or background, while preserving the product, offer and recognizable brand direction. Generate the assets at the original aspect ratio and explain what each version changes. Treat my catalog facts and the attached creative as the source of truth. Keep the real product shape, proportions, construction, print, color, logos and readable labels intact. Do not invent product features, claims or reviews.

FAQs:
Q: What is creative fatigue in Meta ads?
A: Creative fatigue is when the same audience has seen an ad so often that it stops responding. The usual signs are a frequency above about 3, a click-through rate that falls while spend holds, and a creative that has run for several weeks. The ad is not broken; people have stopped noticing it.
Q: What creative refresh strategies work best for fashion?
A: Change the scene, not the garment. A new opening frame, a closer crop on a detail or a new background makes the ad look new, while the cut, print and color stay exactly as they are. Shoppers then see the same product they will receive.
Q: How do I know which ads need a refresh?
A: The daily Meta ad decisions routine marks an ad for refresh when its ad set frequency is above 3.5, or when its click-through rate falls for three or more days while spend holds. Start with those ads.

# E-commerce Analytics: What to Measure and Benchmarks by Vertical
URL: https://www.gotolstoy.com/blog/ecommerce-analytics-what-to-measure-benchmarks-by-vertical
Author: Tolstoy Team | Published: 2026-11-16
Summary: Median AOV and refund rate by vertical from Tolstoy store data, what an online store should measure, and what event counts can and cannot tell an AI agent.

Quick answer: Across Tolstoy's benchmark stores, median AOV (items after discounts, without shipping and tax) runs from $60 in Food & Beverages (112 stores) to $217 in Home (120). The median share of orders with a refund runs from 2.1% in Food & Beverages (102 stores) to 5.8% in Fashion (319). These are medians, not targets: compare a store with its own past, then its vertical. Windows and exclusions: see the table . Why measuring the right thing matters This post is for an AI agent that builds an online store, and for the person who directs it. Once the store ships, the next question is whether it works, and the agent answers with whatever it measured. With nothing measured, it cannot tell a pricing problem from a returns problem, or a good month from a bad one. With the wrong thing measured, it gives a confident wrong answer, in one of four ways: The wrong comparison. The same AOV reads differently by vertical: $95, the 25th percentile of Home stores, is above the Beauty & Wellness median ($62) and below the Fashion median ($122). An agent that judges a store against the wrong vertical, or compares an AOV that includes shipping with a benchmark that does not, recommends the wrong change. The wrong window. A refund rate taken on last week's orders is not comparable with the table's, where every order had 30 to 89 days for a refund. The wrong unit. A step rate built on event counts instead of shoppers counts every repeated add to cart as if it were another shopper. The wrong inference. A feature whose users buy more has not been shown to work; its users may have been more likely to buy anyway. Each of these produces a number that looks like a result and points the store at the wrong fix. Benchmarks by vertical: AOV and refund rate These are medians across stores that send Tolstoy their orders. They are published in Tolstoy's ecommerce-analytics agent skill and were read from Tolstoy's warehouse on 2026-11-16. Store-level medians of AOV and refund rate by vertical. Stores that joined after April 2026 have no classification. A vertical with fewer than 30 stores is left out. The AOV and refund columns have separate store counts. Middle half: the 25th to the 75th percentile of stores. AOV: each store's revenue ÷ its orders, for orders from 2026-08-18 to 2026-11-15 (90 UTC days). Revenue is the order's items after discounts, without shipping and tax. Refund rate: each store's share of orders with a refund above zero, partial or full. Orders from 2026-08-18 to 2026-10-16, refunds up to 2026-11-15, so each order had 30 to 89 days for a refund. Stores with no refund in the window (88 of 1,512) are left out, because Tolstoy may not receive their refunds. Pets: no refund benchmark is published. No conversion-rate benchmark: Tolstoy does not see a store's total visits, so it cannot compute a store's conversion rate. What the table shows (descriptive reading) This section is a descriptive reading of the published table: what its medians and quartiles show for these stores and windows. It does not explain why a vertical looks the way it does, it does not describe the full distribution beyond the 25th percentile, median and 75th percentile, and none of it is evidence that any feature or tool changes these numbers. Inside a vertical, AOV spreads widely; Home most of all. Home has the highest median AOV ($217) and the widest middle half ($95 to $582): a Home store at the 75th percentile has more than six times the AOV of one at the 25th. The Home median alone therefore says little about where one Home store should sit. Health has the narrowest AOV middle half ($44 to $94, a $50 span). Four verticals have close AOV medians. Food & Beverages ($60), Pets ($61), Beauty & Wellness ($62) and Health ($69) have medians within $9 of each other, and each of these four verticals' middle half contains all four medians. The table does not show how far the store distributions overlap beyond that. It does show that for these four the gap between medians is smaller than the spread inside each vertical, whose middle half spans $50 or more. Refund medians differ by vertical, and Fashion's quartiles are the highest. Fashion's median refund rate (5.8%) is more than twice Beauty & Wellness's (2.2%) and Food & Beverages's (2.1%). Fashion's 25th percentile (2.8%) is above the medians of Food & Beverages, Beauty & Wellness, Health (2.6%) and Sports & Outdoors (2.7%), and its 75th percentile (11.8%) is the highest in the table; its middle half, 9.0 points wide, is also the widest. Refund rate here counts orders with any refund, partial or full; it does not say how many dollars were refunded. AOV and refund rate rank verticals differently. Home has the highest median AOV but a lower median refund rate (4.3%) than Fashion (5.8%). Sports & Outdoors has the second-highest median AOV ($129) and the fourth-lowest of the eight median refund rates (2.7%). Food & Beverages has the lowest median of both ($60 and 2.1%). In this table, one metric does not stand in for the other, so track both. Some rows rest on few stores. Beauty & Wellness has 621 stores for AOV. Pets has 30, the minimum for a vertical to be published, and no refund benchmark; Baby & Kids (51 stores for each metric) and Sports & Outdoors (57 and 55) are also small. Quartiles of 30 to 57 stores are less settled than those of several hundred; read them as rough. The windows and exclusions are part of the numbers. AOV uses orders from 2026-08-18 to 2026-11-15; refund rate uses orders from 2026-08-18 to 2026-10-16, with refunds counted to 2026-11-15, so every order had 30 to 89 days in which a refund could be recorded. A refund rate on orders that had less time is measured over a shorter window: on the same orders it can only count the same or fewer refunds, so it is not on this table's definition. Compare refund rates on orders of the same age. The 88 of 1,512 stores that reported no refund are left out; removing the lowest values can keep a median in place or raise it, never lower it. Every store here sells in USD, had at least 30 orders in the window and did not join after April 2026; a new store with a handful of orders is outside this population. How an agent should use these numbers Compare the store with its own previous period first, of the same length, with the same weekdays, and with no sale or launch in only one of the two. Then match the definitions before placing the store in its vertical's middle half: AOV on items after discounts, without shipping and tax; refund rate as the share of orders with any refund, on orders that had 30 to 89 days; USD only. A number outside the middle half is worth a look at the definitions first, then at prices and returns. It is not a verdict, not a target, and not proof that anything worked. What to measure, and why Revenue = sessions × conversion rate × AOV, where conversion rate is orders ÷ sessions and AOV is revenue ÷ orders. A change can raise revenue only through one of those three terms, so name the term a change is meant to move before shipping it. Refund rate sits beside them: it is the share of orders that were partly or fully refunded, not the share of revenue refunded. For refunded dollars, use the refund amounts in the store's order data. Metric Formula Take it from Orders, revenue Count and sum of orders in the period Store platform Average order value (AOV) Revenue ÷ orders Store platform Conversion rate Orders ÷ sessions Store platform Buyer rate Shoppers who ordered ÷ shoppers who visited Event counts (shoppers) Orders per buyer Order events ÷ order shoppers Event counts Step rate Shoppers at a step ÷ shoppers at the step before Event counts (shoppers) Refund rate Orders with any refund ÷ orders Store platform Each of these rates is meaningful because its numerator and denominator are defined units over the same period. The trap is mixing them. Conversion rate divides orders by sessions from the store platform; buyer rate divides shoppers by shoppers from event counts. They answer different questions, so neither substitutes for the other, and a change in one says nothing exact about the other. Raw event counts are not shoppers: add-to-cart events ÷ product-view shoppers is not a step rate, because one shopper can add to cart many times. A ratio also needs its numerator and denominator to match in definition, population, period and currency; whether they come from the same tool matters less. Orders from the store's order data divided by sessions from its analytics are a valid conversion rate when both cover the same storefront and the same days in the same time zone. The ratio breaks on a mismatch: orders that include sales the sessions never saw, such as another sales channel, orders for one set of days against sessions for another, or revenue in two currencies added as one. And a revenue figure needs its scope stated: with or without discounts, shipping and tax. For the storefront, a small event plan is enough: page_view when any page shows, product_view when a product page shows, add_to_cart only after the cart accepts the item, checkout_started when checkout opens, and order_completed once per order on the confirmation page. Give each name one meaning, write it down in the store project, and never rename it, because a new name starts a new count. If checkout is hosted and runs no store code, the store cannot send order_completed ; take orders and buyers from the store platform instead. What event counts can and cannot tell you The E-commerce Analytics SDK (the TolstoySDK package) sends storefront events from the browser, and Tolstoy's report gives two numbers per event name for a period of whole UTC days, up to 180 days: events , how many times it was sent, and shoppers , how many different shoppers sent it. Every rate is computed by the agent from these counts, and each one is a ratio of two counts, not the share of one confirmed group of shoppers. That has consequences: It is not a strict funnel. add_to_cart shoppers ÷ product_view shoppers does not check that the same shoppers did both. A buyer can skip a step, return in another browser, or take the first step before the period started. Ask for a period much longer than the time between the two events so that these edges stay small. Identity is per browser, and only with consent. The SDK keeps one shopper ID per browser. Where the store has a consent tool, it sends no event until the shopper allows analytics and drops the events from before that. Counts cover only browsers that allowed analytics, and one person on two devices is two shoppers. Both sides of a ratio share these limits. Shoppers do not add up across reports. A shopper is counted once per report, so daily shopper counts do not sum to a weekly one. Ask for the whole period in one report. Zero and missing differ. 0 is a measured zero. A missing name was not sent in the period, or is not among the 120 most frequent names in the report. There is no revenue in the events. The report does not show, group or sum parameters, so an order value sent as a parameter never becomes revenue or AOV. Those come from the store's orders, as do the benchmarks above, not from the event report. Correlation is not effect. Shoppers who choose to open a size guide often were more likely to buy anyway, so a higher buyer rate among them is a correlation, as is a before-and-after comparison around a launch. To estimate an effect, show the feature to a random half of shoppers, compare the halves, and judge the 95% range of the difference rather than each rate; when that range includes zero, there is no shown effect. The ecommerce-analytics skill gives the formula and how to credit an order to a feature. Adding it to a store The docs state that sending events and reading the report are free on every Tolstoy plan, the free plan included, and that events never count toward Shoppable Videos view billing. No Tolstoy widget is needed. Two facts shape the plan: sign-up and the approval of the CLI or MCP sign-in happen in a browser, so an agent without one needs its person for those steps; and the report covers whole UTC days before today, with today's events showing from about 06:30 UTC tomorrow. The SDK takes the public app key, not the secret API key. Setup, consent handling and the same-day delivery check are in the Tolstoy e-commerce analytics guide , with reference in the Tolstoy SDK , Tolstoy CLI and Connect your agent pages. Installing the ecommerce-analytics skill in the store project, and recording the event plan in its AGENTS.md , lets the next agent read the numbers with the same definitions.

# How to Add Shoppable Video to Shopify (Step by Step, 2026)
URL: https://www.gotolstoy.com/blog/how-to-add-shoppable-video-to-shopify
Author: Tolstoy Team | Published: 2026-11-01
Summary: Add shoppable video to your Shopify store in six steps: install an app, connect the catalog, add video, tag products, publish the widget, and measure results.

Quick answer: To add shoppable video to Shopify, install a shoppable video app such as Tolstoy from the Shopify App Store, connect your store so products import, and add videos from Instagram, TikTok or your own files. Then tag products in each video, publish a widget to your product page with the app embed and theme block, and track views, clicks and add-to-carts. Last updated: November 3, 2026. Shopify can show video in product media, but a plain video does not let a shopper buy what they see. Shoppable video adds product tags and an add-to-cart button inside the video, so the shopper can buy without leaving it. This guide uses Tolstoy for the exact steps. The same order of work applies to most Shopify video apps; to compare them, read the best Shopify video apps or the best Videowise alternatives . Before you start Pick the first page. Start with one product page template or your best-selling products, not the whole store. Collect 5 to 10 videos. Short vertical videos that show the product in use work best: creator clips, Reels, TikToks, product demos or customer videos. Confirm rights. Use only videos you own or have permission to use. This is important for creator and customer content. Measure the baseline. Note the conversion rate and mobile page speed of the pages you will change. Step 1: Install a shoppable video app Install Tolstoy from the Shopify App Store . Installs from the Shopify App Store include a 14-day trial. Every account starts on the Free plan. Paid plans start at $16/month billed yearly, or $20 monthly. See pricing . Step 2: Connect your store and confirm the catalog import In Tolstoy, go to Profile → Settings → Set up store . Enter your .myshopify.com domain, select Connect to Shopify , and approve the permissions in Shopify admin. Keep that tab open until Tolstoy confirms the connection. Product import can take a few minutes. Before you continue, confirm that products from the correct store appear in Tolstoy. The Shopify connection guide has screenshots. Step 3: Add your videos You have three ways to fill your library: Import from social. Connect Instagram or TikTok and import videos into your Library. See how to turn Instagram and TikTok videos into shoppable videos . Upload your own files. Upload product demos, brand videos or creator files you already have. Generate new video. If a product has no video, AI Studio can make product video and images from your catalog. Review each result against the real product before you publish it. Step 4: Tag products in each video Tagging connects a video to products in your catalog, so the product card and add-to-cart button appear in the video. Tag each video one at a time, or select several videos and tag them in bulk. Follow these rules: Tag only products that the video clearly shows. Tag the specific variant when the video shows one color, size or style. Put the most relevant product first when you tag more than one. Tags save automatically. The tagging guide covers bulk tagging. Step 5: Choose a format and publish it to your theme Create a widget and pick the format for the page: Product page: stories or a carousel near the product media. See Shopify PDP shoppable video widgets . Homepage: a carousel or a featured video. Collection pages: a carousel of videos for that collection. Site-wide: a floating video or pop-up. Then choose Publish in Tolstoy. For the first publish, enable the Tolstoy app embed in your Shopify theme. Copy the widget code, add the Tolstoy Builder block to the theme template you want, paste the code, preview the page on desktop and mobile, and save. If your theme does not show the block, use the widget code from the publish flow or contact Tolstoy support. Step 6: Measure and improve After a week or two, compare the pages with video against your baseline. Track views, clicks, add-to-carts and attributed revenue per video, not only views. Replace videos that shoppers skip, and move the best videos to more pages. Tolstoy also runs A/B tests in the media gallery, so you can check whether a video changed conversion. Reuse the same videos on more channels When a video sells on your product page, use it again. From the same Tolstoy library you can publish to Shop App and TikTok Shop, put shoppable video in Klaviyo email, and publish approved ads to Meta with Ads Studio . Common mistakes to avoid Too many videos at once. Start with one strong widget and expand when you see results. Wrong product tags. A tag for a product that the video does not show loses the shopper's trust. Long videos. Keep product-page videos short and show the product in the first seconds. No mobile check. Most shoppers watch on a phone, so preview every widget on mobile. Ready to start? Install Tolstoy on Shopify , or compare options first in Tolstoy vs Videowise and Tolstoy vs Moast .

A shoppable UGC platform collects customer and creator photos or videos, secures permission to use them, tags the products shown, and publishes the content on your store, so shoppers can open or buy a product straight from the post. It is software that turns customer and creator content into content a shopper can buy from. For what UGC is and why stores use it, see UGC in ecommerce . A shoppable UGC platform does six jobs, in this order: Collect. It pulls in photos and videos from social accounts, hashtags, review requests or uploads. Get rights. It asks the creator for permission and records the answer. Moderate. It filters out off-brand, low-quality or unsafe content before anything goes live. Tag products. It links each post to the products, and the variants, that the post shows. Publish. It places the content on product pages, collection pages, the homepage or email. Measure. It reports how shoppers engage with the content and what they buy next. The three kinds of shoppable UGC platform Most tools start from one kind of content. Customer UGC vs creator content vs AI UGC Customer UGC is content that customers post on their own. It works as social proof because a real buyer made it. Creator content is paid or gifted. Rights and permission: what to check before you publish Before a customer post goes on your store, check these five things: Written consent is recorded. A like or a tag is not consent. Keep the creator's yes in writing. Where use is allowed. Onsite, ads and email are different uses. Record which ones the creator agreed to. Expiry and revocation. Know when the permission ends and how the creator can withdraw it. Credit or handle shown. Show the creator's handle or name if your agreement says you will. An audit trail. Keep a record of each request, each answer and the date. Vendors use two common request patterns. How to measure shoppable UGC Engagement rate: the share of shoppers who see the content and interact with it, for example by playing, swiping or opening it. Product-tag click-through: the share of content views that lead to a click on a tagged product. Add-to-cart from content: add-to-cart actions that start from the content. Conversion rate, engaged vs not engaged: the conversion rate of sessions that interacted with the content compared with sessions that did not. Shoppers who engage are often closer to buying already, so this gap alone does not prove the content caused the difference. Average order value (AOV): the order value of sessions that engaged with the content compared with sessions that did not. For a fair result, run an A/B test or a holdout on the product page. Show the content to one group and not to the other, then compare conversion rate and AOV. Next step: See how shoppable video works . On Shopify? Compare Shopify UGC apps .

# Clear AI Fashion Model Provenance and Digital-Replica Consent Before Catalog Casting
URL: https://www.gotolstoy.com/blog/ai-fashion-model-provenance-digital-replica-consent
Author: Tolstoy Team | Published: 2026-10-01
Summary: How catalog, creative, and legal ops decide whether an AI on-model identity is synthetic, a digital twin, or a licensed face — before generation runs at catalog scale.

Quick answer: cast the identity on paper before you cast it in production AI fashion model provenance is the record of where each reusable on-model identity came from — fully synthetic, a digital twin of a real model, or a general-purpose face — plus the consent or license that says how far you may use it. Establish that record before a generation run, not after the identity is on thousands of product pages. Catalog teams have mostly settled whether AI on-model imagery is good enough to publish. The question that stalls a rollout now sits earlier in the process, and it is not a creative question: who is the person in the image, and who said you could use them that way. Three casting paths, three different counterparties. A synthetic identity, a real model's digital twin, and a vendor's general-purpose face each need different paperwork. Provenance is a record, not a watermark. It tracks the origin of the identity, not what you tell shoppers about the image. Consent has a shape. Markets, channels, duration, exclusivity, derivatives, and what happens at the end of the term. Clear it before the run. Garments can be regenerated. A face that has shipped across a catalog cannot be quietly recalled. Where it fits: casting is the stage before everything described on AI fashion catalog production at scale . This is an operations checklist, not legal advice. The point of running it is to arrive at your counsel with a clear picture of what you are about to do, rather than a question. Why unclear provenance surfaces late and costs more Nothing about an uncleared identity fails at generation time. The images come back usable, the batch passes review, and the SKUs publish. The problem appears later, from outside: A model or an agency recognizes a likeness in a catalog nobody told them about. A vendor's terms turn out to exclude a market, a channel, or paid media — after the assets ran there. An identity reaches its consent end date while the product pages using it stay live. A supplier or agency delivered generated imagery whose identity source nobody on your side can name. A marketplace or retail partner asks for the provenance of an image and there is no answer to give. Scale is what converts each of these from an incident into a project. The reason to cast a reusable identity at all is reuse: the same face across categories, colorways, seasons, channel resizes, and the long tail. That reuse is the point, and it is also the blast radius. Withdrawing one identity means finding every SKU, every collection page, every channel export, and every ad variant that carries it — including the copies that left your systems. Regenerating a garment is a batch job. Replacing a face is a catalog migration. Three casting sources, in plain language Before anything else, decide which of these each identity in your library is. Most teams discover they already have a mix and have never written it down. 1. Fully synthetic identity An identity created to resemble no specific real person. There is no individual with rights in the likeness, which removes the talent consent question — and replaces it with vendor questions. What to establish: how the vendor produced the identity and what it was built from; whether the identity is exclusive to you or shared across the vendor's customers; whether you may keep using it if you leave the vendor; whether a seed, reference set, or identity file travels with you; and what the vendor warrants if the identity turns out to resemble a real person closely enough that someone objects. The quiet risk here is not consent, it is accidental resemblance and shared reuse. "Synthetic" is a claim about intent, not a guarantee about outcome. 2. Digital twin of a real model A likeness of an identifiable person, built from their images or their participation. This is the path with the richest paperwork, because a real person is on the other side of it and their agreement is the whole basis for the use. What to establish: a signed agreement from the model covering the creation of the replica and its use; the scope of that use; compensation for reuse rather than for the original session alone; whether the model's agency has to approve; what training or likeness basis you are allowed to retain; and the exact end-of-term behavior — stop generating, stop publishing, delete, or something in between. Digital replicas of working models are the subject of active, changing rules in several markets. New York's Fashion Workers Act, which took effect in June 2025 and requires written consent for a model's digital replica, is one example; it is not the only one, and which rules apply to you depends on your talent, your agencies, and the markets you sell in. That mapping is counsel's call, not a production decision. Your job is to arrive with the facts: who, what likeness, which markets, which channels, how long. 3. General-purpose or stock-style face An identity supplied by a vendor, library, or platform for general commercial use — whether it originates from a real person who licensed their likeness or from a synthetic set. What to establish: the license terms in writing, read rather than assumed; whether paid media and marketplace syndication are included or carved out; territory and term; whether the identity is non-exclusive, which it usually is; and whether the license chain runs all the way back to a real person if one is involved. The practical cost of this path is sameness. A non-exclusive face is available to anyone, including the brands you compete with on the same marketplace. That is a brand decision before it is a legal one. What "provenance" means for catalog ops Provenance here is an internal record attached to an identity, carried forward onto every asset generated from it. Three things belong in it: Source of identity. Which of the three paths, and specifically which vendor, model, agency, or library. Likeness or training basis. What the identity was built from, and what you are permitted to keep. License or consent chain. The documents, their scope, their dates, and who holds them. Two things are deliberately not in that list. Provenance is not shopper-facing disclosure — what you tell a customer about an image is a separate decision with its own rules per market and channel. Provenance is also not content authenticity metadata or channel-level synthetic-media tagging; those travel with the file and answer a different question. Keep all three, but keep them separate, because they have different owners and different failure modes. An image can be correctly labeled for shoppers, correctly tagged for a marketplace, and still carry a face nobody cleared. Attach the record to the identity, not to individual images. An identity library with provenance on each entry answers "can we use this face here?" in seconds. A pile of images with metadata answers it after an audit. The digital-replica consent checklist For any identity that is a likeness of a real person, write the scope down in these terms. Vague consent is the failure mode, not missing consent. Who. The model, and the agency or representative whose approval is also required. What. Creation of a digital replica, and generation of new imagery from it — stated separately, because agreeing to one is not agreeing to the other. Where. Territories and markets, named. Which channels. Owned PDP, marketplaces, retail partners, email, organic social, paid media, print. Check paid media and marketplace syndication explicitly; do not assume an owned-channel grant covers them. How long. A term with an end date, and what happens to live assets on that date. Exclusivity. Whether the identity may be used by anyone else, and whether category exclusivity applies. Derivatives. Edits, retouching, restyling, pose and expression changes, video, and whether the likeness may be combined with other identities. Categories and context. Any product types, claims, or contexts the model excludes — intimates, swim, medical, political, or anything else named. Compensation for reuse. How generated volume is paid for, not only the original session. Withdrawal. Whether the model may withdraw, on what notice, and what you must do when they do. Retention. What you keep after the term — the replica, the reference set, the generated assets — and what you delete. Sign-off. Named owners in creative and in legal, with a date. One signature from one side is not a cleared identity. Every line in that list is a question production will ask later. Answering them at casting time is the entire saving. The casting-to-publish workflow Provenance work belongs in a fixed position in the pipeline — before generation, not beside it: Choose the casting path. Synthetic, digital twin, or general-purpose, decided per identity and per use. Clear the paperwork. Consent or license in hand, scope written down, counsel's confirmation on anything new. Lock the identity library. Each entry carries its provenance record, its scope, and its dates. Only cleared entries are available to production. Generate. Run SKUs against the cleared identity and the saved creative direction. Review. Check each output against its source product — the garment-fidelity gate. Publish. Approved assets go to PDP and channels, carrying a link back to the identity that produced them. Re-check on change. New market, new channel, new product category, or an approaching end date sends the identity back to step two. Step 6 is the one teams skip and regret. If a published asset cannot be traced back to its identity, you have provenance at casting and none at withdrawal, which is the moment you need it. The stages after generation — intake standards, saved direction, batching, and review — are covered in how to produce on-model catalog photos at high-SKU scale , and the review gate itself in garment-fidelity QA before the PDP . What this is not Several adjacent problems get confused with this one. Keeping them apart is what makes each of them tractable. Not shopper disclosure. Telling customers an image is AI-generated is a separate obligation with its own per-market and per-channel rules. It says nothing about whose face it is. Not marketplace synthetic-performer tagging. Channel-level metadata requirements are something you comply with at publish time. They are downstream of casting, not a substitute for it. Not brand consistency. Locking models, lighting, styling, and crop so a catalog reads as one brand is a creative-direction problem. A perfectly consistent identity can be an uncleared one. Not diversity casting. Deciding which identities your catalog should represent is a brand and merchandising decision. Provenance applies to whichever identities you choose. Not model swapping. Recasting an already-published set is a migration problem with its own sequencing. This checklist is what you run so that migration is a choice rather than a response. When to pause, and when counsel owns the call Pause generation when any of these is true: Nobody can name the source of an identity already in the library. The plan covers markets, channels, or product categories the consent or license does not name. A consent term ends inside the expected life of the assets about to be generated. Imagery arrived from a supplier, agency, or partner with no provenance attached. A synthetic identity is reported to resemble a real person. A model or agency asks a question you cannot answer from the record. Counsel owns the call on which rules apply to your talent and your markets, on the wording of any replica agreement, on what withdrawal and retention must mean in practice, and on anything involving a real person's likeness in a new market. Production owns bringing them a complete, specific picture: which identities, which path, which scope, which channels, which dates. The failure pattern is not teams ignoring legal. It is teams reaching legal after the run, with a question that now has thousands of published answers attached to it. Where Tolstoy fits In Tolstoy AI Studio, the models, styling, lighting, and crop a brand uses are saved once as reusable direction, and every SKU is generated against that saved direction from an approved flat lay, packshot, or supplier photo. Because the direction is defined once and reused, the identities it carries are a short, reviewable list rather than something re-decided prompt by prompt — which is exactly what makes a provenance record practical to keep. Every output is reviewed against its source product before it is approved, and nothing publishes on its own. Tolstoy does not provide talent clearance, consent documents, or legal review; those stay with your creative and legal owners. What the workflow gives you is a fixed place for the identity decision to live, upstream of thousands of generated assets. Start with the identities you already have Before casting anything new, list every on-model identity currently appearing in your live catalog and mark each one as synthetic, digital twin, general-purpose, or unknown. The unknown column is the work. For most teams it is shorter than expected and older than expected, and clearing it is the cheapest version of this exercise you will ever run.
